fields.title: Descartes Matrix: four questions instead of an argument
fields.keyTakeaway: Before comparing ideas, ask not only “what happens if we do it”, but also “what happens if we don't”. The second question almost always changes the order.
fields.checkQuestion: Two ideas look equally useful. Which question will pull them apart?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key question of the node: **which ideas should be developed further?** Not “which is better”, but which one is worth testing now.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** Ideas are compared by expected benefit, and all ideas look useful — otherwise they wouldn't have been proposed. The choice is made based on who speaks more persuasively.
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **What will happen if we do it?** — expected benefit. This is usually the only question asked.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **What won't happen if we do it?** — cost: what we won't do instead, what will break.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **What will happen if we don't do it?** — cost of inaction. Urgency hides here.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **What won't happen if we don't do it?** — what we won't learn and which door will close.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Idea A: book recommendations on the home screen. Idea B: giving the first book in full with no time limit.

On the first question, both look the same: “people will read more”.

The third question sets them apart. If we don't do recommendations — nothing changes; users already find books through search. If we don't offer the open first book — we will never find out if duration is the issue, and this question blocks three more hypotheses about the trial period.

The fourth question added the decisive point: recommendations can be added at any time, but the window for the trial period experiment is closing — the pricing grid changes in a quarter.
fields.blocks/3/title: Vetka: two ideas with equal benefit
fields.blocks/4/text: The matrix helps unpack a single idea and scales poorly to twenty: four questions for each means an hour for five ideas. A longer list requires a rougher filter, while Descartes is applied to finalists. And it does not produce numbers: the result is understanding, not a score.
